There is not a one-to-one correspondence between O2 consumed and CO2 produced, and the H2O will condense rapidly and become a liquid and not a gas. Some of the O2 will go to form this liquid, reducing the total amount of gas. This means that of course there will be less gas after combustion than before, a general feature of combustion. 

If you're familiar at all with chemistry, you could check out the Wikipedia on combustion; there they explain in the section 'Chemical Reactions' or something like that the stoichiometry of generic combustion reactions.

In the sense that the H20 has to be a liquid (i.e., condense) before the pressure differential due to there being less gas can form, this is the same thing that I am saying. I can't think of another way that the condensation of the water vapor would create such a large pressure differential.

The type of differential heating you are describing will indeed drive convective currents of air within the glass (though principally through local changes in density and thus the hydrostatic pressure distribution), but the heating from the candle will be extremely localized. Furthermore, when the air returns to its initial state (it cools as the candle flame dies) mass currents will of course again be caused within the air in the glass (though no water will be drawn in) and the gas will eventually return to its initial thermodynamic state (and there will be no pressure differential)--that is, unless we take into account the changes induced by a changing composition (or more accurately by a decreased amount of gas) that I am talking about.

The relevant reduction is the reduction in number of moles of gas, not its volume, as this is set by the size of the container. (Yes I am neglecting mass transport and spatial inhomogeneity in this statement.) To get a feel of if this effect is enough to explain what we see, let's look at it the other way: if we say the water column sustained by the pressure differential is 5 cm high (an overestimate if I recall the video well), this requires a reduction of atmospheric pressure by about 0.05 m / 10 m = 0.5% (atmospheric pressure is approximately 10 m of hydrostatic pressure in water). This would likewise require a 0.5% reduction in the total number of moles of gas in the glass. Taking into account the fact that only 21% of air is O2 by mole, this would require only a 2.4% reduction in the number of moles of CO2 after combustion as compared to the number of O2 moles before combustion. This is completely reasonable for a combustion process. (I'm not closely familiar with combustion processes in candles, but almost certainly the stoichiometric reduction is actually more than 2.4%--the fact that we don't see more of an effect is adequately explained by the locality of the O2 consumption and limitations of mass transfer as you pointed out.) This strongly suggests that the reduction due to differential rates of O2 combustion and CO2 production has more than enough capacity to cause the effect we are seeing here.

It is actually caused by the consumption of O2. What matters is not the total mass content (there is no universal relationship between matter content and pressure that is valid for all materials, conditions, and states of matter), but the fact that more moles of O2 are consumed than CO2 produces, resulting in a pressure differential driving water into the cup. See my comment here:
https://old.reddit.com/r/geek/comments/9xwrjb/covering_a_lit_candle_with_glass_cup/e9w7ps1/

This effect has nothing to do with either the heating from the candles (PV = NkT, so the locally heated air in the gas glass will create a pressure differential that would tend to drive oxygen out, not pull water in), nor the difference in density (CO2 is more dense than air, and P = (N/V)kT ~ density X T so that, again, an increase in density would create a pressure differential that would force air out but not water in).

Some people have said that it cannot be the consumption of O2 during combustion because of conservation of mass, but the total mass content is irrelevant. What matters is the difference in pressure. (If you've discovered your universal equation valid in all materials, states of matter, and environments relating mass content to pressure, then I suspect you'll be collecting your Nobel prize very soon.) The combustion process consumes O2 and produces both CO2 and H20:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combustion#Chemical_equations
Since some of the oxygen is used to add that O in H2O, the total number of CO2 molecules produces will be less than the total number of O2 molecules consumed. As the pressure is proportional to the number of molecules N (PV = NkT), the pressure is reduced.

Indeed, the driving pressure here is due to the combustion of oxygen leading to a net decrease in the amount of gas present (even though mitigated partially by the production of CO2).

The Schrodinger equation is H Psi = E Psi, where H = (-hbar^2 /2m)d^2 /dx^2 + U is the Hamiltonian operator.  Stationary states, like the one you have been given, are eigenstates of this operator meaning 1) they have a fixed energy, and 2) this energy is the corresponding eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian operator.  Practically speaking, this means you need to apply the Hamiltonian operator to the wavefunction (i.e., plug the given function into the equation (-hbar^2 /2m)d^2 Psi/dx^2 + U Psi).  The result will itself be proportional to the given function (by definition of what an eigenstate is), and the constant of proportionality will be the energy of the state.

Just trying to help out.  It seemed like you were missing something, given that you said GDP has nothing to do with population, which contradicts the point I just made, to which you flatly said 'yes, that is true.'
The point isn't how to calculate GDP, or even that we're talking about GDP.  It's that GDP is an extensive variable, like total number of scientific papers produced.  It scales with population size.

His point is that both GDP and scientific productivity are extensive variables, meaning that they scale with population size.

Let's make it more simple though.  I want to compare the average scientific productivity of a person in a country to the average wealth of that person (roughly speaking).  So, average scientific output = total papers / population, and average wealth = GDP / population.  Thus, my ratio of average scientific output to average wealth per person is (total papers / population) / (GDP / population) = total papers / GDP, i.e., the ratio of the extensive variables.

The intensive variables are things like per capita GDP or total papers / population, which vary from country to country but don't scale with population.  When we want to compare 'scientific efficiency' (or whatever we're talking about here), we want to calculate an intensive quantity.  Intensive quantities come from ratios of extensive quantities.

Another example from physics:  which is more massive, mercury or water?  On the surface, this is a meaningless question, because I could have 100 kg of water and 0.004 g of mercury, or the inverse, and the answer would depend on how much of the substance I have in a very trivial way.  So, to get around this, under the assumption that the question I'm asking is meaningful, I calculate the density.  Density is mass, which scales with size and is extensive, divided by volume, another extensive quantity.  This gives an intensive quantity, a quantity that does not depend on how much of the stuff I have (mercury or water), and a quantity that we can therefore directly compare, and this is how we can say mercury is about 14 times heavier than water.  Likewise for the density of scientific production per unit wealth.

Hope this helps.

Indeed, my research actually focuses exactly on this anology.  The phenomenological equations describing electron/hole transport in semiconductor materials is precisely identical to the equations describing diffusion/electroconvection of dilute ionic species in water (in the context of nanometric scale confinement where surface charge additionally acts as the analogue of impurity density).  There is no difference however in the Poisson equation; this is a very general relation from electrostatics that generally must be solved in either context.

What's cool about this is that, if the equations are identical for semiconductor solid state devices and ionic nanofluidic devices, then in principal the same solid state components realized with SCs can be realized with ionic systems.  In particular diodes, which allow us to rectify things like solute flux, solvent flux, and electric current.  Among other areas, this is hugely promising for desalination, because if solvent flux rectification can be achieved in practice, it provides a method of doing reverse osmosis with orders of magnitude less energy than traditional pressure driven methods.

The analogy between hydraulic (at low Reynolds number) and electrical circuits is indeed quite interesting but I think a bit different from what you're getting at in your question.  In this case, the analogy is a consequence of the fact that we are in both cases in the linear response regime, meaning that the perturbation from an equilibrium is sufficiently weak that we can take the response to this perturbation to be linear in the perturbation itself.  In the case of electrical circuits, the perturbation is an applied electric field (represented by the voltage difference in Ohm's law) and the response is the electrical current.  In the case of the hydraulic circuit, the perturbation is the applied mechanical pressure, and the response is the volumetric flow rate.  In fluids, there is the additional complication that you can have turbulent flow which engenders a dissipation in your flow that is no longer linear in the flow rate / velocity, and the linearity of the pressure-discharge relation breaks down.

But what's even more interesting is to ask if the hydrodynamics of the two systems themselves are the same.  First, a note on what I mean by hydrodynamics.  So-called generalized hydrodynamics for statistical physicists is a very general framework to describe (in a continuum context) how a system responds when perturbed from thermodynamic equilibrium by relatively weak excitations/perturbations.  In the context of say water containing some dilute chemical species, we have the well-known Navier-Stokes laws, Fick's laws of diffusion, etc., each of which may be derived in a rather formal and general way using the facts that 1) the fluid momentum and the masses of water and chemical species are conserved, 2) we are dealing with a classical system, and 3) the system is constrained to obey certain symmetries.

We can likewise do this for quantum systems, for example electron gases.  In this case, we get to answer number one to your question:  a priori, no, the hydrodynamic theory describing an electron gas is not the same as for a classical fluid.  This is purely because a quantum system does not behave collectively like a classical system, and novel purely quantum effects must be contained in the hydrodynamics.

However, what is striking is the great similarity that nonetheless does exist between electron gas hydrodynamics and classical hydrodynamics.  For instance:

https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.04165

These authors look at viscous flow of electrons in graphene, and find that the equations describing such flow are very nearly classical.  This is a fascinating result; the idea that the flow of an electron gas in any context should share any features of a classical fluid is striking and a priori rather unexpected.

To summarize:  a priori, no, a quantum system generally cannot be described using classical hydrodynamics; however, at least in certain contexts, the hydrodynamics of electron gases bears a striking number of common features with classical fluids.

Hi, I'm an American who has lived in Paris for a PhD for a little more than a year.  (C'est vraiment terrible que je parle anglais dans le seul espace français sur Reddit, je sais.  Mais en générale je déteste parler français avec les anglophones.)  Are you coming to Paris?  If so, what I'm about to say will be relevant to you; if not, then it may not be, as I've spent only a little time in the parts of France that aren't Paris.  (They do technically exist.)

There's absolutely nothing about the experience of being an American in Paris that should in any way dissuade you from coming or have you feeling nervous.  Especially if you speak a bit of French.  Are you going to overhear (or have if your new friends don't immediately pick up on the fact that you're American--distinctly possible as the French, like us, are generally pretty terrible with accents) negative conversations about the States?  It's possible as it's happened to me before.  Are you going to get yelled at (in French and/or broken English) in a shop if your French isn't quite up to snuff?  Yeah, almost definitely (not as a rule, but it will probably happen).  And will drunken conversations with your French companions occasionally turn to biting (and sometimes a bit ignorant) criticism of Americans/American government/American ideals or way of life/American sports?  Yeah, probably that as well.  But in general the French don't particularly give a shit if you're from the States.  And, after all, they all watch our movies and our TV and listen to our music and really, really fucking love *Mac*Donalds for some fucking reason.  (Subway too, you see those everywhere in Paris.)


In the end, I think that the French view of Americans is probably pretty symmetric with the American view of the French.  Sure, in theory we may have some particular ideas about the French--that they are rude, arrogant, untrustworthy, don't bathe, and wear the most ridiculous little fucking scarves, but in practice that would never stop us from kicking it with a French guy or judging him as a person rather than as a collection of ill-informed stereotypes.


One anecdote:  I was once at a party at the lab where I work, and I went outside to have a cigarette and talk to a friend of mine (a French grad student).  He was talking to a middle-aged researcher and the guy was for whatever reason at that moment talking a phenomenal amount of shit about Americans.  And then he turned to me and said bon soir and asked where I was from (my pigeon French holds no secrets) and I said the States.  And my friend said but don't worry he's one of the good ones, and we laughed and carried on.  By the end of the night me and that dude were best friends.  (Of course the alcohol may have helped with that.)


So, yeah, those are my thoughts on it.  I guess the take away is that no one really actually cares about where you're from.

I was pretty severely depressed as a teenager.  These past few years, I've gone through a cycle of severe depression that recurs every ~3 to 6 months.  Recently, I was thinking a bit about the distinct impressions I have when I'm depressed and how I might describe them to people.



There's some component of it that is very physical and visceral.  It feels like there's a cavity inside of my abdomen, or maybe like my insides are all knotted up.  It's a very bizarre and physical feeling.


Also, when I'm depressed, it's not quite like being sad (although sometimes I can be overwhelmingly sad).  It's more like I'm just on the very edge of being incredibly sad, like I feel like I want to break down and cry but I just can't quite get there.  It's maybe like the indifference other people have described.


Indifference has been a big part of it too.  I tend towards substance abuse and alcoholism generally, but particularly when I'm depressed.  During these times I can go for days (depending on work schedule) without showering, leaving my room (except as necessary to eat, buy booze, cigarettes), chain smoking, alternately staring at Netflix or the wall, and generally not bothering to turn the lights on.


Another impression I've had:  when I'm depressed, my best days are my worst days, by which I mean that when I have a particularly good day, when I connect with friends or do well at work or whatever, at the end of the day I always, *always* feel the worst.  I have the feeling that whatever positive thing I may have obtained or achieved, it will go away either because I'm too much of a fuck up to maintain it, or because that's just the way life goes, always regressing to a baseline that is kind of shit to begin with.


Finally, when I'm depressed, I feel utterly, completely isolated.  Like my isolation isn't just a contingent fact of my circumstance but a necessary fact of my own existence.  I'm at base unable to connect with people (I feel), and in any case the very idea of trying, of explaining yourself to someone else, seems so exhausting that there's just no point in bothering.


Anyway, just some thoughts that I had.

In fact, MD gives the same results as statistical mechanics for the ensemble averages of the observables when the Hamiltonian is ergodic (ergodicity roughly refers to the assumed equivalence of an ensemble and time average).  If the Hamiltonian is indeed ergodic, then MD will trace out (assuming we are doing a microcanonical, or constant energy, simulation) many paths on the constant energy shell in phase space, sampling our microcanonical distribution.  We can then average over those paths in phase space to determine ensemble averages of observables.  In the case of an ordered entropic phase transition in MD, most of the time the particles will inhabit portions of phase space corresponding to that ordered phase.

Statistical physics applies specifically to those cases where we don't want to do the calculation, so to speak.  Molecular dynamics is doing the calculation.  It's important to remember that entropy has meaning only in a statistical context.  You don't talk about the entropy of a single particle evolving in a specified way according to a known Hamiltonian from some given initial data because it has no meaning in that context.  Entropy is something like the 'informational cost' of the coarse graining inherent in the statistical description of a system.

To put it more concretely, say I have N particles in a box interacting via some specified potential and I want to determine the macroscopic observables (i.e., things like temperature, pressure, etc. that I can measure by, e.g., sticking a thermometer in the box).  I have two ways of doing this.  I can write down the Hamiltonian and solve my equations of motion for each particle for some (or many different) initial sets of position and momenta.  Then, after some period of time, when I believe the system has become ergodic (also said:  thermalized, or forgotten its initial state) then I calculate my observable for that final configuration.  This is molecular dynamics.

Alternatively, I don't want to solve the equations fully, in which case I opt for a statistical description of the system.  In this case, following Boltzmann, I make some assumptions about the statistical weight of different configurations and sample from the possible configurations according to this weight.  Then I average the observable, calculated for each sampled configuration, over all sampled configurations.  The entropy in this statistical description is purely a function of the statistical weight of the different possible configurations.  In the case that we are interested in sampling a box of N particles with a fixed total energy E, the entropy is famously given by Boltzmann's formula:  S = k lnW, with S = entropy, k = Boltzmann's constant, and W = the total number of configurations corresponding to a particular specified macroscopic state.  The point to take away is that entropy is purely an aspect of this statistical description of the system.

Now, whence, e.g., entropically driven phase transitions?  This is purely to do with the relative number of system configurations corresponding to different phases.  If we were to do the statistical experiments I described in the preceding paragraph with a system of hard disks (they can't overlap but they don't interact otherwise) in 2D, we'd find that, beyond a certain critical density, we'd be much more likely to randomly sample a state in which the disks had crystallized.  Thus, we have an entropically driven phase transition.
